items.title: Hillcrest Farmers Market
items.description: Sunday market with more than 175 vendors. Produce, prepared food, flowers, crafts. Parking fills up by 10 and the surrounding blocks get slow. Go early if you want the good stalls.

items.title: Hillcrest Car Show
items.description: Classic car meetup on the third Saturday of every month. Owners park up, everyone walks the row and talks shop. It moved off Normal Street to Fifth and Pennsylvania while the promenade is under construction.

items.title: Disco Craft Paint and Sip
items.description: Guided craft night at the winery. Around 34 dollars, materials included.

items.title: Noche De Cuba at Negociant
items.description: Havana themed evening at the winery. Around 18 dollars to get in.

items.title: The Hillcrest sign went up
items.description: A group of women shopkeepers put up the neon sign in 1940 to draw shoppers to the business district. It is 21 feet long, weighs 800 pounds, and started out lit by 240 feet of pink neon tubing. It fell into disrepair and was rebuilt in 1984, and that relighting party is what became CityFest. In 2023 it was retrofitted with color changing LEDs.

items.title: The Hillcrest Pride Flag
items.description: Sixty five foot flagpole at Normal and University, raised in 2012. It works as the unofficial center of the neighborhood and the gathering point when something happens.

items.title: The Brass Rail moved to Hillcrest
items.description: San Diego's first gay bar opened downtown in the 1930s and relocated to Fifth and Robinson in the early 1960s. It is still open, which makes it one of the longest running gay bars in the state.

items.title: The San Diego LGBT Community Center opened
items.description: One of the first LGBTQ community centers in the country, founded in the early 1970s. It still runs social services out of a former union hall and is the neighborhood's civic anchor.

items.title: Sears closed and became the Uptown District
items.description: Sears ran on this block from 1952 until March 1986. The city bought the 14 acre site for 9 million dollars and turned it into 318 homes plus retail. It drew national attention as one of the first compact pedestrian oriented mixed use redevelopments in the country.

items.title: The Kahn Building
items.description: Built in 1919 during the Egyptian Revival craze. It runs the length of the block to Sixth Avenue. Look up at the frieze, most people walk past it every day without noticing.

items.title: Streetcars ran down University Avenue
items.description: Trolleys once ran down the middle of University Avenue and turned north on Normal Street toward the teaching school. Nothing on the street tells you this now, which is part of why it is worth marking.

items.title: The Pride parade route
items.description: Since 1993 the parade has run from Hillcrest along University and Sixth into Balboa Park. It draws more than 250,000 spectators, over double Comic Con, which makes it the largest civic event in the city.

items.title: CityFest took over Fifth Avenue
items.description: The annual street festival ran noon to 11pm across roughly seven blocks of Fifth Avenue, with two stages, a kids zone, and more than 70,000 people through the day.

items.title: Quince Street footbridge
items.description: A wooden trestle pedestrian bridge over the canyon, one of the quiet ways into Balboa Park on foot. Locals use it, visitors mostly never find it.

items.title: Upas Street footbridge
items.description: The other hidden pedestrian crossing linking the neighborhood to the park. Good shortcut, better view.

items.title: Vermont Canyon path
items.description: Canyon trail at the south end of Vermont Street. One of several green cuts running through the neighborhood that most people never walk.

items.title: Richmond Canyon staircase
items.description: Reached by a staircase one block south of Pennsylvania. Steep, shaded, and completely invisible from the main streets.

items.title: Irving Gill built here
items.description: Gill put up his Arts and Crafts influenced designs in the neighborhood in the early 1900s. There is also work by Hazel Waterman and Lillian Rice, two of the first women to practice architecture in the country. Replace this pin with specific addresses once you find them.

items.title: Jimmy Wong's Golden Dragon
items.description: The neighborhood's oldest continuously operating restaurant, marked by a vintage neon sign just west of the Hillcrest gateway. It was remodeled in 2006 and reopened as Asian Bistro.

items.title: Normal Street Promenade under construction
items.description: The block is being rebuilt as a permanent home for the farmers market. Worth photographing now, because nobody is recording what this looked like during the build.
